cards.explanation: The answer is True. Mordecai walks in because Esther had revealed his relation to her. Esther's the queen, and she opens the door by saying who he is to her. Family connections still get you in the room, friends, even in a palace.

The answer is the signet ring. The king had recovered it from Haman, the man who plotted against the Jews, and now he takes it off and presents it to Mordecai. Later the king says a decree written in his name is sealed with the royal signet ring (Esther 8:8). That's a whole lot of trust to slide across the table, friends.

The answer is True. The text says Esther appointed Mordecai over the estate of Haman. The king gave her the estate, and she puts Mordecai over it. Mordecai raised her (Esther 2:7), and now she hands him the keys. I bet that felt good.

The answer is an order revoking Haman's letters. Esther asks that an order be written to revoke the letters Haman wrote to destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces. Haman, the one who schemed against them, is gone, but his letters are still out there. She doesn't ask for something for herself, friends. She asks for her people.

The answer is destruction. Esther says, "How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?" She asks it right after asking how she could bear to see the disaster that would befall her people. Those two questions are the heart of her plea, friends.

The answer is to write as they please in the king's name. The king says, "Now you may write in the king’s name as you please regarding the Jews, and seal it with the royal signet ring." He's giving Esther and Mordecai the pen and the ring, friends. That's about as much freedom as a king can hand out.

The answer is False. The king says, "For a decree that is written in the name of the king and sealed with the royal signet ring cannot be revoked." So Haman's sealed letters (Esther 3:12) can't just be taken back. What the king does say is that Esther and Mordecai may write in his name as they please regarding the Jews and seal it with the ring.

The answer is Mordecai. The royal scribes recorded all of Mordecai's orders to the Jews and to the satraps, governors and princes. He's the one with the ring now, and these scribes are writing down what he says. I think those scribes got a serious hand cramp that day.

The answer is True. The scribes write to each province in its own script and to every people in their own language. The Jews get it in their own script and language too. That's a lot of alphabets to keep straight, friends.

The answer is couriers on swift royal horses. Mordecai sends the documents by mounted couriers riding on swift horses bred from the royal mares. The letters are going to 127 provinces (Esther 8:9), so those horses had a lot of road ahead of them. Delivery by hoof, friends.

The answer is to assemble and defend themselves. The king permitted the Jews in each and every city the right to assemble and defend themselves. Assemble and defend, those are the two words to hold on to. And it's a right for the Jews in each and every city, friends.

The answer is so the Jews will be ready on that day. A copy of the edict was to be published to all the people, so that the Jews would be ready on that day. The day is set, and now they know about it ahead of time. Knowing the day is half of being ready, friends.

The answer is True. Mordecai goes out from the king's presence in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. This is the same Mordecai who walked in the front door only because Esther told the king who he was. Now he walks out looking like that, friends.

The answer is False, friends. The text says Mordecai went out from the king's presence in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen (Esther 8:15). Then it says the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced. Rejoiced is the word the text uses, not confused.

The answer is that they become Jews themselves. The text says many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them. The text gives that fear as the reason. That's a big turn from where this story started, friends.
